collection_summary: Adapted / narrowed from seed #21 in datasets/pkdb_bench/docs/example_questions.txt ('For each major world religion, list its 5 holiest sites with their city, country, and a brief note on why each site is significant.'), narrowed at staging time to the four largest religions per Wikipedia 'Major religious groups' (Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism) and reframed at cycle-1 audit from 'top 5 holiest sites' to 'five major holy or pilgrimage sites' (because the cited Wikipedia articles do not consistently define ranked top-5 holiness orderings across all four religions). Tier B (manual_wikipedia) extraction, with per-site Wikipedia articles cited for Islam after the cycle-1 audit identified an LLM-generated-content warning on the consolidated 'Holiest sites in Islam' article (November 2025). The instance is the first PKDB-Bench instance in the Religion family. Schema is (Religion, List Position, Site, City, Country, Significance Note) with composite PK (Religion, Site) (cycle-2 audit fix; was (Religion, List Position) in cycles 0-1); 4 religions x 5 sites = 20 rows. List Position is retained as a non-key 1-5 ordinal that records the order in which sites are listed in the cited per-religion source. Multi-attribute (Site, City, Country, Significance Note) over a per-religion partition exercises the calibration goal of scaled_enumeration: the universally cited top-3 of each religion (Mecca/Medina/Jerusalem in Islam; Holy Sepulchre/St. Peter's/Santiago in Christianity; Ayodhya/Mathura/Haridwar in Hinduism per Sapta Puri article order; Lumbini/Bodh Gaya/Sarnath in Buddhism) are very widely known, while sites at positions 4-5 (Cave of the Patriarchs, Imam Ali Shrine, Lourdes, Jasna Góra, Varanasi, Kanchipuram, Kushinagar, Rajgir) are progressively less universally known and exercise the confidence gradient.
source_coverage_notes:
Nine Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the universe + per-religion selection + per-site values. Cycle-1 audit fixes: replaced the consolidated 'Holiest sites in Islam' article (LLM-content-flagged Nov 2025) with five per-site Wikipedia articles for the Islam rows; replaced 'Hindu pilgrimage sites' with 'Sapta Puri' as the more direct anchor for the Hindu universe + canonical-order rule.

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_religious_groups): universe. Defines the 4-religion universe by adherent count from the largest-groups table; flags 'folk religion' and 'unaffiliated' as excluded due to heterogeneity / non-religion.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_pilgrimage): selection + value (Christianity rows). Identifies the 'three great pilgrimages of Christendom' (Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago) per Pope Alexander VI tradition plus Lourdes and Jasna Góra as the article's most-emphasized modern Catholic pilgrimage centers; supplies one-sentence significance phrasing.
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram): selection + value (Islam row 1). Confirms Mecca's Masjid al-Haram as 'the most significant mosque in Islam' and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Masjid_an-Nabawi): selection + value (Islam row 2). Confirms Medina's Prophet's Mosque as 'the second largest mosque and second holiest site in Islam after the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca'.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa_Mosque): selection + value (Islam row 3). Confirms Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque as 'the third holiest in Islam, after Mecca and Medina'.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_the_Patriarchs): selection + value (Islam row 4). States 'according to some sources, the mosque is the 4th holiest in Islam' while qualifying that 'other sources rank other sites as 4th' — captured in the Significance Note. Also serves Christianity / Judaism cross-reference (the site is revered by all three Abrahamic traditions).
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imam_Ali_Shrine): selection + value (Islam row 5). Identifies the shrine as 'the fourth holiest Islamic site' for Shia Muslims and the burial site of Ali ibn Abi Talib. Confirms only Mecca/Medina/Karbala/Mashhad receive more annual Muslim pilgrims.
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapta_Puri): selection + value (Hinduism rows). Defines the seven holy cities of Hinduism (Ayodhya, Mathura, Haridwar, Varanasi, Kanchipuram, Ujjain, Dwarka) in the article's canonical order; the staged Hinduism rows take the first five in this order. Notes Varanasi as the 'most holy of the seven sacred cities' and supplies one-sentence significance phrasing for each city.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_pilgrimage_sites): selection + value (Buddhism rows). Defines the Four Holy Sites identified in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar) and the supplementary 'Eight Great Places' (which extends the Four with Rajgir, Vaishali, Sravasti, Sankassa); the staged Buddhism rows take the Four Holy Sites in chronological order (birth -> enlightenment -> first sermon -> parinirvana) plus Rajgir as the most prominent supplementary site.

Validation note: source_urls[5] (Cave of the Patriarchs) carries an explicit 'some sources / other sources' qualifier on the 4th-holiest claim — the Significance Note cell preserves this hedged phrasing, and the audit should accept any answer that captures the 4th-holiest-with-disagreement nuance. Source_urls[6] (Imam Ali Shrine) also has 'citation needed' tags in some sections but the 'fourth holiest Islamic site' claim is sourced.

Universe-size sanity: the 4-religion universe matches the largest groups in Wikipedia 'Major religious groups' (Christianity > Islam > Hinduism > Buddhism); folk religions (~0.2B) is the next-largest group but lacks a unified holy-sites list and is excluded by the 'coherent tradition with shared holy sites' criterion. The 5-per-religion partition matches the seed's 'list its 5 holiest sites' phrasing (now reframed to 'five major holy or pilgrimage sites' per cycle-1 audit).
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks. R1: 'major world religions' has no canonical list — anchored to Wikipedia 'Major religious groups' largest-groups table. R2: 'top 5 holiest sites' is fuzzy across denominations — cycle-1 audit reframed as 'five major holy or pilgrimage sites' rather than 'top 5 ranked holiest', and the column was renamed Rank -> List Position. R3: the 'Significance Note' column is qualitative free-text; cell-level evaluation should accept semantic similarity rather than exact-string match. 20 rows >> the 10-row floor; 6-column shape with 1 partition key + 1 list-position ordinal + 1 entity key + 3 non-key text attributes; strong confidence gradient (universal top-3 vs less-known 4-5); LLM-knowable for major sites; low temporal sensitivity.
- Seed/provenance: ADAPTED / NARROWED from seed #21 in example_questions.txt (line 35). The seed text is 'For each major world religion, list its 5 holiest sites with their city, country, and a brief note on why each site is significant.' Two adaptations relative to the verbatim seed: (a) cycle-0 staging narrowed 'each major world religion' to 'each of the four largest world religions (Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism)' to match the Wikipedia 'Major religious groups' largest-groups universe; (b) cycle-1 audit reframed 'list its 5 holiest sites' to 'list five major holy or pilgrimage sites' because the cited Wikipedia articles do not consistently define a ranked top-5 holiness ordering across all four religions.
- Category: scaled_enumeration — primary because the instance is a per-partition selection (5 sites per religion) with multiple non-key attributes and a confidence gradient. The composite PK is (Religion, Site) (cycle-2; was (Religion, List Position) in cycles 0-1) because List Position is curator-listed display order rather than a source-defined ranking. The union+filter operation_type follows the precedent of the only other staged scaled_enumeration instance (top_grossing_films_worldwide_per_decade_1980s_2010s), which has a true ranking criterion (worldwide gross).
- Source plan: 9 Wikipedia URLs across universe (Major religious groups), Christianity (Christian pilgrimage), Islam (5 per-site articles after cycle-1 audit replacement), Hinduism (Sapta Puri after cycle-1 audit replacement), Buddhism (Buddhist pilgrimage sites). Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention.
- Expected shape: 4 x 5 = 20 rows x 6 cols, composite PK (Religion, Site) (cycle-2; was (Religion, List Position) in cycles 0-1). Realized: 20 x 6, 0 duplicates.
- Domain: Religion/Holy Sites — NEW family per domain_taxonomy.md.
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above, all addressed by source-anchoring decisions and the cycle-1 reframe.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Christianity selection: chose the 'three great pilgrimages of Christendom' (Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago) historical ordering from Pope Alexander VI tradition plus the two highest-emphasis modern pilgrimage centers (Lourdes, Jasna Góra) per the Wikipedia 'Christian pilgrimage' article. Bethlehem (Church of the Nativity) is universally significant but is not in the article's top-5 by emphasis and is a top-10 expansion candidate. Reframed at cycle-1 as a 'selection' rather than a 'ranking' because the Wikipedia article does not enumerate a definitive ranked top-5.
2) Islam selection: top-3 (Mecca/Medina/Jerusalem) is universally Sunni+Shia and corroborated by the per-site Wikipedia articles (each individually states its respective ranking position). List positions 4 and 5 (Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf) are anchored to the per-site articles' explicit 4th-holiest claims (with the Cave of the Patriarchs article explicitly noting 'other sources rank other sites as 4th'). The 4-5 mix across Sunni and Shia traditions is honest about the cross-tradition disagreement. Cycle-1 audit replaced the consolidated 'Holiest sites in Islam' source with these five per-site articles because the consolidated article carries a Wikipedia LLM-generated-content warning (Nov 2025). The cycle-1 fix uses individual per-site Wikipedia articles, each of which independently supports its row.
3) Hinduism selection: cycle-1 audit fix — uses the FIRST FIVE of the Sapta Puri article's canonical order (Ayodhya, Mathura, Haridwar, Varanasi, Kanchipuram). The cycle-0 staging had Hinduism rows in a different order (Kashi at position 1 instead of position 4) which was inconsistent with the Sapta Puri article's first-5 ordering. Cycle-1 re-ordered the Hinduism rows to match the Sapta Puri article. The Site column uses Sanskrit canonical names (Kashi, Maya) while City uses modern English names (Varanasi, Haridwar) — for Ayodhya / Mathura / Kanchipuram the Sanskrit and modern names match.
4) Buddhism selection: chose the Four Holy Sites identified by the Buddha himself in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Lumbini / Bodh Gaya / Sarnath / Kushinagar) plus Rajgir as the most prominent supplementary 'Eight Great Places' site per the Wikipedia article. Order is chronological (birth -> enlightenment -> first sermon -> parinirvana -> teaching). Reframed at cycle-1 as a 'selection' rather than a 'ranking' because the Mahaparinibbana Sutta defines a Four Holy Sites set rather than a definitive top-5 ranking; Rajgir at position 5 is curator selection from the Eight Great Places set.
5) Schema: composite PK is (Religion, Site) (cycle-2 audit fix; was (Religion, List Position) in cycles 0-1). Column 'Rank' was renamed 'List Position' at cycle-1 to honestly reflect that the column records the order in which sites are listed in the cited per-religion source, not an absolute holiness ranking. At cycle-2 the audit found that List Position was still acting load-bearing as part of the PK even though it is not consistently source-defined (Buddhism in particular has chronological row order in the CSV while the cited 'Buddhist pilgrimage sites' article emphasizes Bodh Gaya first); cycle-2 moved List Position out of the PK and into a non-key 'numeric' column (was 'rank' type). The Site column is now the load-bearing per-religion entity key. List Position is retained as a non-key display ordinal so readers can still see the curator-listed order.
6) Country normalization: standard country names. Country handling for contested territory: 'Israel' for Old City Jerusalem sites (Holy Sepulchre, Al-Aqsa); 'Palestine' for West Bank sites (Hebron). 'Vatican City' is used for both city and country for St. Peter's Basilica because Vatican City is a sovereign state.
normalization_decisions: Religion names use English Wikipedia article-title forms (Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism). Site names use the Wikipedia article title where possible (Masjid al-Haram, Mahabodhi Temple, Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, Cave of the Patriarchs (Ibrahimi Mosque)). City names use Wikipedia's primary modern English form. Country names are the standard short forms. Country handling for contested territory: 'Israel' for Old City Jerusalem sites (Holy Sepulchre, Al-Aqsa) per Wikipedia convention reflecting de facto administration; 'Palestine' for West Bank sites (Hebron / Cave of the Patriarchs). 'Vatican City' is used for both city and country for St. Peter's Basilica because Vatican City is a sovereign state. The Significance Note column is a one-sentence paraphrase of the cited article's description and uses Wikipedia article phrasing where direct quotes were given (e.g., 'three great pilgrimages of Christendom', 'most significant mosque in Islam', 'second largest mosque and second holiest site', 'third holiest in Islam', 'fourth holiest Islamic site' for Shia, 'most holy of the seven sacred cities'). Where the cited Wikipedia article uses hedged language (e.g., 'according to some sources, the mosque is the 4th holiest in Islam' for the Cave of the Patriarchs), the Significance Note preserves the hedged phrasing rather than asserting a flat 4th-place ranking. Sort order is (Religion ASC, List Position ASC). Cycle-1 audit fix: column 'Rank' was renamed 'List Position' to honestly reflect that the column records the order in which sites are listed in the cited per-religion source, not an absolute holiness ranking. Cycle-2 audit fix: composite PK changed from (Religion, List Position) to (Religion, Site), and List Position column type changed from 'rank' to 'numeric'. The PK change reflects that Site is the load-bearing per-religion entity identifier; List Position is curator-listed display order and is not consistently source-defined as a ranking (e.g., Buddhism rows are in chronological order — Lumbini-Bodh Gaya-Sarnath-Kushinagar-Rajgir — while the cited 'Buddhist pilgrimage sites' Wikipedia article emphasizes Bodh Gaya first; either ordering is defensible from the source, and the cycle-2 PK change avoids the need to commit to one order as canonical).
open_questions: 1) The Religion-family target is 5 instances per instance_selection_priorities.md; this is the first. Future Religion-family instances could include 'major religions x liturgical languages', 'world religions x founding dates', or 'religions x estimated adherent counts'. 2) Christianity's selection by 'Christian pilgrimage' article emphasis (Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago, Lourdes, Jasna Góra) excludes Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity even though it is universally significant. Bethlehem is a top-10 expansion candidate. 3) The Hindu list uses the FIRST FIVE of Sapta Puri article order (excluding Ujjain and Dwarka). An alternative would be to include the full Sapta Puri (7 cities) — that would change the per-religion partition shape from 5 to 7. Document the first-5 choice. 4) The Buddhist 5th-site choice (Rajgir) is the most prominent of the supplementary 'Eight Great Places' but not canonical in the same way as the Four Holy Sites. Alternative 5th-site choices include Sravasti, Vaishali, or Sankassa. 5) Country normalization for Old City Jerusalem ('Israel') vs Hebron ('Palestine') follows Wikipedia convention; the audit should accept semantically equivalent variants ('Israel/Palestine', 'Palestinian Territories', etc.) for these contested-territory rows. 6) The 'Significance Note' column is qualitative free-text; benchmark evaluation should treat semantic similarity to the cited Wikipedia phrasing as success rather than exact-string match. 7) The 4-religion universe is anchored to Wikipedia 'Major religious groups' largest-groups table; folk religions (~0.2B) is excluded because it lacks a unified holy-sites list. Adding Sikhism, Judaism, or Bahá'í would require a different universe anchor and is a candidate expansion. 8) cycle-1 audit reframed the instance from 'top 5 holiest ranked' to 'five major holy or pilgrimage sites selected'. A future instance could attempt the ranked framing using stronger per-religion ranking sources, but each religion's 'holiness ranking' is genuinely fuzzy beyond the universal top-3, so the selected framing is more honestly source-defined. 9) Source_urls[5] (Cave of the Patriarchs) and source_urls[6] (Imam Ali Shrine) carry minor 'some sources / other sources' or 'citation needed' caveats; the Significance Note cells preserve the hedged phrasing.

blocking_addressed: Scope/title mismatch — the cycle-0 title 'list its 5 holiest sites' implied a ranked top-5 holiness ordering, but the cited per-religion Wikipedia pilgrimage / holy-sites articles do not consistently define such a ranking across all four religions. Cycle-1 fix: reframed table_title to 'list five major holy or pilgrimage sites' (selection rather than ranking) and renamed the schema column 'Rank' to 'List Position' to honestly reflect that the column records the order in which sites are listed in the cited per-religion source, not an absolute holiness ranking. db_analog updated to reference list_position. claim_type stays source_defined; the source defines the universe and the article-emphasized selections, not a definitive ranked top-5.

Hinduism row order — the cycle-0 staging claimed 'first 5 of Sapta Puri' but the row order (Kashi at position 1, Mathura at 2, Maya at 3, Ayodhya at 4, Kanchi at 5) did not match the Sapta Puri article's canonical order (Ayodhya, Mathura, Haridwar, Varanasi, Kanchipuram, Ujjain, Dwarka). Cycle-1 fix: replaced the cited Hindu source 'Hindu pilgrimage sites' with the more direct 'Sapta Puri' Wikipedia article (which is clean of LLM-content warnings) and re-ordered the Hinduism rows to match the article's first-5 canonical order. Hinduism row 1 is now Ayodhya (was Kashi); row 4 is now Kashi (was Ayodhya). The 5 cities are unchanged; only the within-religion ordering was corrected.

Islam source quality — the cycle-0 staging cited the Wikipedia 'Holiest sites in Islam' article, which carries a Wikipedia LLM-generated-content warning (added November 2025) prohibiting its use as a reliable benchmark grounding source. Cycle-1 fix: replaced this single consolidated source with five per-site Wikipedia articles, one per Islam row: Masjid al-Haram, Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, Al-Aqsa Mosque, Cave of the Patriarchs, and Imam Ali Shrine. Each per-site article independently supports its row's ranking claim ('most significant mosque', 'second holiest', 'third holiest', 'some sources rank as 4th holiest', 'fourth holiest Islamic site' for Shia). source_count moved from 5 to 9 to reflect the additional per-site URLs. None of the five per-site articles carry LLM-content warnings (some have routine citation-needed or dispute tags on unrelated sub-claims, which are normal Wikipedia maintenance flags).
hygiene_addressed: Cycle-1 audit hygiene cleanup: rewrote collection_summary, source_coverage_notes Roles: block, decision_log items 1-5, normalization_decisions, _extraction_notes, and temporal_note in draft.json to consistently use 'selection' / 'List Position' language rather than 'ranking' / 'Rank' language. The cited Significance Note phrasings preserve hedged source language (e.g., 'some sources rank the mosque as the 4th holiest' for the Cave of the Patriarchs) where the source carries such qualifications.

blocking_addressed: Structural — List Position was still part of the composite PK after cycle-1, but the cycle-1 reframe moved the table from 'ranked top-5 holiest' to 'selected five major sites'. Keeping List Position in the PK implied a load-bearing within-religion ordering that is not consistently source-defined: the Buddhism rows are in chronological order (Lumbini -> Bodh Gaya -> Sarnath -> Kushinagar -> Rajgir per the Mahaparinibbana Sutta canonical order) while the cited Wikipedia 'Buddhist pilgrimage sites' article emphasizes Bodh Gaya first. Cycle-2 fix: changed PK from (Religion, List Position) to (Religion, Site); changed column_types['List Position'] from 'rank' to 'numeric'; updated db_analog to drop the ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY) windowing (which implied a computed ranking) and read as a flat selection table ordered by religion + list_position. PK uniqueness verified: 20 unique (Religion, Site) tuples. No CSV row data changes. The Site column is now the load-bearing per-religion entity identifier; List Position is retained as a non-key display ordinal so the curator-listed order is still visible to readers.
